criterion_notes.c1: The household survey descriptively measures household water and sanitation provision on premises across Mumbai (reporting that 69.4% had piped water on premises and 75.0% had a toilet facility on premises in Table 1), although these are treated solely as independent variables predicting citizen policy priorities rather than as service-access outcomes under investigation.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails under BOTH the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain literal wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility-governance mechanism governing water or sanitation access (such as eligibility rules, documentation or tenure requirements, tariffs, administrative burden, enforcement, or regulatory structure) is examined; the authors explicitly state they do not address formal and informal infrastructure governance or urbanization stakeholders. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the survey operationalizes 'socio-institutional' / 'local area governance conditions' solely as education/literacy and voluntary citizen participation in residential action groups, neighbors' associations, or social networks, and tests these only as predictors of subjective citizen policy-priority rankings rather than water or sanitation service access; accordingly, plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary quantitative empirical study based on 1,261 household surveys conducted across more than 30 Mumbai neighborhoods between December 2013 and February 2014, reporting univariate frequencies and bivariate odds ratios.
criterion_notes.c4: No water or sanitation service-access outcome is evaluated. Household piped water on premises and toilet facility on premises are entered strictly as independent variables (Section 5.1, Table 1), whereas the study's dependent variables (Section 5.2, Tables 2–4) are citizens' subjective rankings of their top three policy priorities (such as ranking air pollution, waste and sewage management, water and sanitation, or extreme heat as a top-three priority).
criterion_notes.c5: Within its own research question, the population and unit of analysis (1,261 surveyed households/respondents in Mumbai), independent variables, dependent priority-ranking outcomes, and cross-sectional survey design are clearly identifiable, though the exposures and outcomes do not meet review scope criteria c2 and c4.

raw_response.exposure: Local household conditions treated as independent variables: socio-demographic and civic-participation factors (sex, age, education/literacy, household durable assets, and participation in residential action groups, neighbors' associations, or social networks), household infrastructure provision (clean cooking fuels, 24-hour electricity, piped water on premises, toilet facility on premises), and health conditions (acute health episode in the past year, chronic asthma).
raw_response.outcome: Citizen subjective rankings of top-three urban infrastructure and environmental policy priorities among ten competing issues (with bivariate odds-ratio analyses focused on whether air pollution, waste and sewage management, water supply and sanitation, and extreme heat were ranked as top-three priorities).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Surveyed households/citizens across more than 30 neighborhoods in the Mumbai metropolitan region, India (1,261 households surveyed in December 2013 and February 2014; up to 15% item non-response across specific variables).
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E03 — Wrong exposure; also fails Criterion 4 on outcome). This cross-sectional survey of 1,261 Mumbai households examines how socio-demographics, household assets, voluntary membership in residential/neighborhood/social networks, existing household infrastructure (including piped water and toilet on premises), and health status shape citizens' subjective rankings of top-three urban environmental and infrastructure policy priorities. It examines no rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (and explicitly notes that it does not examine formal/informal infrastructure governance or stakeholders). Moreover, household piped water and toilet presence are treated solely as independent variables predicting policy-priority rankings rather than as service-access outcomes, so the paper is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional household survey (descriptive frequencies and bivariate odds-ratio analyses)
